title: Enums vs union literals
subtitle: Runtime emit, reverse mapping, as const maps

cards.front: What two TypeScript tools model a closed set of values?
cards.meaning: Enums, which emit runtime objects, and string/number literal unions, which are usually fully erased. Enums remain useful for namespacing and some numeric domains; many modern React/RN codebases default to literal unions or as const objects.

cards.front: What do many React/RN codebases default to instead of enums?
cards.meaning: Literal unions or as const objects. Enums are kept when namespacing or a numeric domain actually needs a runtime object — not as the default for API/DTO string fields.

cards.front: What values do numeric enum members get if you omit initializers?
cards.meaning: They auto-increment from 0: Admin is 0, Editor is 1, Viewer is 2. Role.Admin is therefore 0 at both type and runtime.
cards.example: enum Role { Admin, Editor, Viewer } // Role.Admin === 0

cards.front: What is Role[0] on a numeric enum?
cards.meaning: Numeric enums emit a runtime object with forward and reverse mapping: Role.Admin is 0 and Role[0] is 'Admin'. Role['Admin'] === 0 as well.
cards.notes: Newcomers often confuse Role[Role.Admin], which looks up the reverse name from the numeric value.

cards.front: How does a regular enum compile to JavaScript?
cards.meaning: It compiles to an IIFE that builds a real JS object with forward entries and, for numeric enums, reverse entries. That object is shipped in the bundle unless tree-shaken carefully — often kept whole.

cards.front: What is the bundle cost of a regular enum vs a literal union?
cards.meaning: A regular enum is a real JS object, usually shipped whole. A string literal union type has zero runtime footprint for the type itself — fully erased.

cards.front: What does Object.keys(Role) include for a numeric enum?
cards.meaning: Both member names and the stringified numbers from reverse mapping. Numeric enums are not a clean list of names if you iterate the object naively.

cards.front: How do you iterate a numeric enum without picking up reverse keys?
cards.meaning: Filter with care — a common approach is typeof value === 'string' so you keep names and skip the numeric reverse entries. Unfiltered iteration includes both directions.
cards.notes: Iterating numeric enums without filtering reverse keys is a listed trap.

cards.front: Why is Role[Role.Admin] confusing on a numeric enum?
cards.meaning: Role.Admin is 0, so Role[Role.Admin] is Role[0], which reverse-maps to the string 'Admin'. Newcomers mix the numeric value with the reverse name lookup.

cards.front: Is a string enum erased at runtime?
cards.meaning: No. It is still a runtime object, like a numeric enum. The difference is values are stable strings closer to API payloads — not that it vanishes from the bundle.

cards.front: Do string enums have reverse mapping?
cards.meaning: No. TypeScript does not auto-create Role.ADMIN-style keys from the string values. Only numeric enums add reverse entries.
cards.example: enum Role { Admin = 'ADMIN' } // Role['ADMIN'] is not auto-created

cards.front: How do you typically compare a string-enum value?
cards.meaning: You often still write role === Role.Admin rather than treating any 'ADMIN' string as the same. Whether a loose string counts depends on typing and the enum's somewhat nominal behavior.

cards.front: Can a plain JSON string assign to a string enum?
cards.meaning: Often not without a cast. String enums are somewhat nominal: a plain 'ADMIN' may not be assignable to Role. A literal union type Role = 'admin' | … accepts matching strings after validation more naturally.

cards.front: Is string-enum nominal typing a feature or a pain?
cards.meaning: Both. Stricter assignability can prevent mixing arbitrary strings with Role; the same rule is a pain for JSON interop, where you may need a cast that a literal union would not.

cards.front: What does const enum emit, and what are the tooling caveats?
cards.meaning: Members inline at compile time — no runtime object from classic tsc emit. isolatedModules, Babel, and SWC may forbid or mishandle const enum because they do not see the whole program; you may need preserveConstEnums or should avoid const enum.
cards.example: const enum Direction { Up, Down } const d = Direction.Up; // typically inlines to 0

cards.front: Why is const enum harder to debug?
cards.meaning: Inlined members appear as magic numbers or strings in the output, with no Direction.Up object left to inspect. That is another reason teams prefer literal unions unless they control a tsc-centric pipeline and want inlining.

cards.front: When should you prefer literal unions over const enum?
cards.meaning: By default. Prefer literal unions unless you control a tsc-centric pipeline and specifically want inlining. Const enum plus Babel or isolatedModules is a common breakage.

cards.front: Why do API JSON strings work with a literal union type?
cards.meaning: The type is fully erased and a plain literal like 'admin' is assignable after validation. canEdit('admin') is ok — you do not need an enum member or a cast the way string enums often do.

cards.front: How do literal unions pair with discriminated unions?
cards.meaning: Discriminant tags are themselves literal unions, e.g. status: 'loading' | 'success'. That is the default style — not numeric enums as tags.

cards.front: How do you derive a union from an as const object?
cards.meaning: const ROLES = { Admin: 'admin', ... } as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[keyof typeof ROLES]. You get namespaced ROLES.Admin plus a derived union of the values.

cards.front: Does an as const object map include reverse mapping?
cards.meaning: No. You get a runtime object only if you use it, and it contains only the entries you listed — no numeric reverse map. That is enum ergonomics without enum reverse-mapping surprises.

cards.front: How does as const tree-shaking compare to a regular enum?
cards.meaning: An as const map can tree-shake better if you import individual constants carefully (bundler-dependent). A regular enum object with all members is worse to shake and is often kept whole.

cards.front: How do you derive a union from an as const array?
cards.meaning: const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number] derives the union from a readonly tuple — useful for iteration plus typing together.

cards.front: Comparison table: runtime footprint of enum vs union?
cards.meaning: enum is a real JS object (usually). A union of string literals has zero footprint for the type — fully erased. const enum inlines with tooling caveats; unions are always erased.

cards.front: Comparison table: enum vs union interop with JSON strings?
cards.meaning: Enums often need an enum member or a cast — especially string enums' nominal feel; numeric enums are worse. With a union, 'admin' works with the union type after validation.

cards.front: Comparison table: reverse mapping and tree-shaking?
cards.meaning: Numeric enums have reverse mapping (surprising); unions have none. Tree-shaking is worse for enums because you ship an object with all members; better for unions because there is nothing to ship for the type.

cards.front: Why prefer type Role = 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer' over enum Role?
cards.meaning: Unions are erased — no bundle cost — while regular enums emit a JS object. Literals interoperate with JSON/API strings more naturally. Enums give Role.Admin namespacing and numeric ordering sometimes; for most API/DTO fields, default to string literal unions or as const maps when you want a runtime namespace.

cards.front: When do enums still make sense?
cards.meaning: Existing codebase or library APIs that already expose enums; when you want a runtime object to iterate or display labels and accept the cost; rare numeric protocols with reverse lookup (document carefully); or aligning with a domain that already thinks in enums, such as some Java interop. Otherwise union plus as const.

cards.front: Does switch plus assertNever work with enum vs union?
cards.meaning: Literal unions work cleanly with switch and assertNever. Enums do too (case Role.Admin). With numeric enums, remember reverse-mapping quirks if values are not fixed carefully, and reverse keys when iterating the enum object.

cards.front: Are enums erased like interfaces?
cards.meaning: Regular enums are not — they emit runtime objects. Interfaces and type unions erase. Assuming enums vanish like interfaces is a common mistake.

cards.front: Why not use numeric enums for API roles?
cards.meaning: APIs sending 0/1 for roles are brittle and confuse consumers. Prefer string literals in DTOs and validate at the boundary — fewer mappings than numeric enums.

cards.front: Are enums always banned?
cards.meaning: No. 'Enums are banned' absolutism skips the tradeoff. Default to unions for DTOs; keep enums when you need a runtime namespace, an existing API, or a documented numeric protocol.

cards.front: What is the trap when comparing a string enum to a loose string?
cards.meaning: Assignability is not the same as a literal union. A loose string may not be a Role without a cast, so equality checks and JSON values can surprise you if you ignore the somewhat nominal typing.

cards.front: Three ways to model a closed set of values?
cards.meaning: A literal union (erased), an enum (runtime object), or an as const map (runtime object plus a derived union). Pick from that fork, not from a fourth invented mechanism.

cards.front: Should discriminants be literal tags or numeric enums?
cards.meaning: Default style is literal tags, not numeric enums. Discriminated unions pair with string literal unions; numeric enum tags fight JSON interop and reverse-mapping quirks.

cards.front: Why prefer erasure for React/RN closed sets?
cards.meaning: Bundle size: a type union ships nothing; a regular enum ships an object. React and RN codebases often prefer erasure for that reason, using as const only when a runtime namespace is actually used.

cards.front: What balanced default should you give in an interview?
cards.meaning: Unions for DTOs and API strings; enums when namespacing or a runtime object is wanted. Be ready to show reverse mapping, string-enum vs union interop, const enum tooling caveats, and deriving a union from as const.
